### Load data
```{r}
library(tidyverse)

billboard <- read_csv(file.choose())

glimpse(billboard)
```

### Clean data
```{r}
billboard <- billboard |>
  rename(
    last_week = `Last Week`,
    peak_position = `Peak Position`,
    weeks_on_chart = `Weeks in Charts`
  )
```


### Song's debut date
```{r}
song_debuts <- billboard |>
  group_by(Song, Artist) |>
  summarise(
    debut_date = min(Date, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```



### Each song's peak position 
```{r}
song_peaks <- billboard |>
  group_by(Song, Artist) |>
  summarise(
    peak_position = min(Rank, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

### How many weeks each song was on the chart
```{r}
song_weeks <- billboard |>
  group_by(Song, Artist) |>
  summarise(
    total_weeks = n()
  )
```
### Combine data sets
```{r}
song_summary <- song_debuts |>
  left_join(song_peaks, by = c("Song", "Artist")) |>
  left_join(song_weeks, by = c("Song", "Artist"))
```

### Find each song's debut month
```{r}
song_summary <- song_summary |>
  mutate(
    debut_month = month(debut_date)
  )
```
### Assign month to seasons 
```{r}
song_summary <- song_summary |>
  mutate(
    season = case_when(
      debut_month >= 6 & debut_month <= 8 ~ "Summer",
      debut_month >= 9 & debut_month <= 11 ~ "Fall",
      debut_month == 12 | debut_month <= 2 ~ "Winter",
      debut_month >= 3 & debut_month <= 5 ~ "Spring"
    )
  )
```


```{r}
billboard |>
  summarise(
    earliest_date = min(Date),
    latest_date = max(Date)
  )
```

The data contains information about songs that have been on the Billboard Hot 100 since July 6, 1958 to May, 5, 2022. I organized the data to show the song title, artist, debut date, peak position, total weeks on the chart, debut month and season. The most important columns for my project will be debut date, season, total weeks and peak positions. One important piece of information I am missing, but not sure I really need, is each song's actual release date...since I'm seeing whether the season in which a song first appears on the Billboard Hot 100 chart has a relationship with its success rather than it's actual release date. Streaming numbers could also be interesting data to include as they would help show why certain songs perform better on the chart. I'm wondering how to account for songs that are on the Billboard Hot 100 for multiple seasons. I want to make sure I'm focusing on the season of it's debut rather than the season it became most popular. What do you think is the best way to compare success across seasons and do you think the song's release date and streaming numbers is necessary to include? 

### Test Ideas/Notes
- I think I will filter out songs released after spring 2022 and holiday songs, as Prof. Willis suggested in the comments of the previous project assignment. I'm not sure how I will filter out holiday songs though. 
- Prof. Willis suggested to focus on songs that first made the list in the summer and compare those songs to ones that first debuted in other seasons like this: 

song_summary <- song_summary |>
  mutate(
    debut_month = lubridate::month(debut_date),
    summer_group = if_else(
      debut_month %in% c(6, 7, 8),
      "Summer",
      "Other"
    )
  )
  
  song_summary |>
  group_by(summer_group) |>
  summarise(
    songs = n(),
    mean_weeks = mean(total_weeks, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_weeks = median(total_weeks, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_weeks = sd(total_weeks, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

- I also think I could see if songs that debut in the summer reach higher chart positions than songs that debut in other seasons. We did something similar to this when looking at PG county car accidents as we calculated the averages across different time periods. 

song_summary |>
  group_by(season) |>
  summarise(
    songs = n(),
    mean_peak = mean(peak_position, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_peak = median(peak_position, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

- I'm wondering if songs that debut in the summer are more likely to be a top 10 song compared to songs that debut in other seasons. I asked chatGPT how to run this test because I don't recall doing a similar test in previous assignments. I told chatGPT the data I have in the song summary table and it told me to compare the percent of songs that reached the Top 10 out of all songs that debuted in each season. This would allow me to compare the success rates across seasons even if the amount of songs each season is different. This is the code it gave me:

song_summary |>
  mutate(
    top_10 = if_else(peak_position <= 10, 1, 0)
  ) |>
  group_by(season) |>
  summarise(
    songs = n(),
    top_10_songs = sum(top_10),
    percent_top_10 = mean(top_10) * 100
  )
  
- Like the test above, I could compare songs that reached No. 1 across each season. This is the test I would run:


song_summary |>
  mutate(
    number_one = if_else(peak_position == 1, 1, 0)
  ) |>
  group_by(summer_group) |>
  summarise(
    songs = n(),
    number_one_songs = sum(number_one),
    percent_number_one = mean(number_one) * 100
  )

- Similar to the HW11 assignment where we calculated percentages within a group, I could look at the percentage of songs that stay on the chart for a least 20 weeks. This would help me see if summer songs are more likely to stay on the charts longer. I also asked ChatGPT to help me code this. This is the test it sugguested I run:


song_summary |>
  mutate(
    long_running = if_else(total_weeks >= 20, 1, 0)
  ) |>
  group_by(summer_group) |>
  summarise(
    songs = n(),
    long_running_songs = sum(long_running),
    percent_long_running = mean(long_running) * 100
  )

- In the PG County car accidents assignment, we looked at data from multiple years to see if there was a change. I think I could see if the success of summer songs changed over time by grouping songs into the decade they debuted it and compare the amount of weeks they were on the chart and their peak positions. This would help me see whether summer songs have consistently been more succssful or if their success has changed over time. I asked ChatGPT how to group the songs into decades and it said to use "lubridate::year()" to create a decade column. 

song_summary <- song_summary |>
  mutate(
    debut_year = lubridate::year(debut_date),
    decade = (debut_year %/% 10) * 10
  )

I would then have to compare the songs across decades. 


song_summary |>
  filter(debut_year >= 1958, debut_year < 2022) |>
  group_by(decade, summer_group) |>
  summarise(
    songs = n(),
    mean_weeks = mean(total_weeks, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_peak = mean(peak_position, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
